newsitem.title: USA: Greyhound looks to the skies in marketing strategy.
newsitem.headline: Greyhound looks to the skies in marketing strategy.

text.p: Greyhound Lines Inc figures that if you can't beat the discount airlines at their marketing game, you might as well cooperate with them.

Greyhound -- the oldest U.S. intercity bus service and the only one still operating nationally -- is actively pursuing agreements with low-cost air carriers to aid its recovery from years of losses, said Stuart Robinson, the company's marketing vice president.

The company admits that one of its biggest errors in recent years was trying to compete head on with the low-cost airlines. In the early 1990s, it introduced deep discounts for advance-purchase tickets and raised the price of its walk-up fares. But the strategy alienated existing customers and failed to win new ones.
Now, Greyhound wants to function as an air-route feeder by providing short-haul bus service between airports and towns that are too small to attract commuter air service.
Although he would not name specific airlines, Robinson said several low-cost air carriers have shown interest in Greyhound's proposal.
Progress has been hampered, however, by the reluctance of airports to give permission for Greyhound buses to pick up and drop off passengers at their terminals.
Robinson was not able to say whether Greyhound would be able to launch the short-haul airport service in 1997, but he was optimistic it would begin at some point.
He said it would attract travelers who might not otherwise ride buses, as well as appeal to the company's "transitional" market segment of discretionary passengers.

These customers account for just 40 percent of bus riders, but 60 percent of revenue. They tend to use low-cost airlines for long-distance journeys, but if the distance is not too great, and they don't need a car at their final destination, they'll ride Greyhound.

In early 1995, Greyhound launched fresh advertising aimed specifically at transitional customers with the theme, "Be with the one you want to be with." The Houston office of Ogilvy & Mather Worldwide, an advertising agency owned by WPP Group Plc, handles the creative portion of Greyhound advertising and developed the slogan.
"We try to encourage additional bus trips with an emotional appeal," Robinson said. He also said the new creative work has worked well in stimulating traffic for Greyhound.

Greyhound is in a recovery phase after losing $77 million in 1994 and $17.8 million in 1995. A bitter drivers strike in 1990 and operational mistakes, such as cutting too many ticket sales agents, contributed to the company's woes.

Part of its failure, too, was linked to the strategy of competing with the airlines with low-cost, advance-purchase tickets, the company concedes. That alienated its core market of cash-paying walk-up customers: urban youth, military personnel, widows and retirees.

Robinson said that marget segment is extremely price sensitive. These customers also cannot make advance reservations because they often don't know when they will be able to travel until the last minute, and they don't own a major bank credit card.

Greyhound reversed those missteps in the mid-1990s. It retained some advance-purchase fare discounts, but lowered walk-up fares once again. The company also added to its bus fleet, bringing the current total to 2,100. It began upgrading its terminals and used its new reservations system to offer connections to regional bus lines. Ridership started to rise again.

The company has also stayed with its decades-old advertising theme, "Leave the driving to us," which Robinson said appeals to its core market. Greyhound primarily uses radio with support from television and national magazines.
Greyhound also uses local ethnic newspapers and local television guides to convey specific route pricing messages and to conduct fare sales. "So low you gotta go" is the sale slogan.
